title: Conditional Probability & Bayes Rule
interviewAnswer: Conditional probability updates the probability of an event given evidence. Bayes rule reverses a conditional using prior probability and likelihood, and underlies probabilistic inference and many classifiers.
why: Conditional probability is the language of updating beliefs from evidence. It appears in Bayesian reasoning, diagnostic tests, anomaly detection, Naive Bayes, calibration, and any interview question where base rates matter.
intuition: Think of probability as shrinking the universe of possible outcomes after observing evidence. P(A|B) asks: among the cases where B happened, how often did A happen? Bayes rule lets you reverse the direction when P(B|A) is easier to reason about than P(A|B).
deepDive: Bayes rule combines a prior belief P(A) with the likelihood of evidence P(B|A), then normalizes by P(B). The base-rate term matters: even a highly accurate detector can have poor positive predictive value when the event is extremely rare. Independence means P(A,B)=P(A)P(B); conditional independence can hold even when marginal independence does not, which is why graphical models and Naive Bayes can be useful simplifications.
math:
P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B)
Bayes: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B)
Total probability: P(B)=Σ_i P(B|A_i)P(A_i)
workedExample: Suppose a defect occurs in 1% of parts. A detector catches 95% of defects and falsely flags 5% of good parts. Among flagged parts, the probability of a true defect is far below 95% because the 99% non-defect base rate dominates. This is the classic base-rate lesson.
code:
# Bayes update for a binary diagnostic test
prior = 0.01
sensitivity = 0.95
false_positive = 0.05
posterior = sensitivity*prior / (sensitivity*prior + false_positive*(1-prior))
print(round(posterior, 3))
commonMistakes: Ignoring the base rate and equating sensitivity with P(defect | positive).
Treating conditional probabilities as symmetric: P(A|B) is not generally P(B|A).

production: For rare-event systems such as fraud, failures, or safety alerts, calibration and base rates directly determine alert quality. Thresholds should be chosen using posterior risk and operational costs, not accuracy alone.
